content: Once pushed to the brink, giant tortoises on a Seychelles atoll now outnumber the country’s people, with a new survey estimating nearly 183,000 animals. Aldabra Atoll, home to the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population, supports an estimated 180,000 animals, according to research led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter. The highest estimate yet for the Aldabra giant tortoise ( Aldabrachelys gigantea ) reflects both a remarkable conservation recovery and a better way of counting animals that are difficult to see. Published in Ecology and Evolution , the study analyzed monitoring records collected by SIF staff from 2018 through 2022. It delivers the first rigorous estimate covering the atoll and replaces the widely quoted figure of about 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s. The team’s best estimate was almost 183,000 adult and subadult tortoises, more than the entire human population of the Seychelles. Their numbers appeared relatively stable during the study period. That abundance would have been difficult to imagine in the 19th century, when heavy exploitation reduced Aldabra’s tortoises to fewer than 1,000. Their recovery has been supported by decades of protection, including the atoll’s designation as a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Today, Aldabra and the Galapagos are the two remaining strongholds of native wild giant tortoises, with far fewer animals in the Galapagos. The new findings strengthen Aldabra’s reputation as one of the Indian Ocean’s outstanding conservation successes. “The monitoring data in this study were collected by SIF staff living and working on the atoll, year after year. More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra,” said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF. The larger total comes with an important qualification: it does not mean the population has nearly doubled since 1999. A tortoise can be present without being visible, and earlier surveys did not adequately account for animals concealed in scrub or shade. Those estimates probably missed a substantial number. To address that problem, the researchers used Bayesian hierarchical distance sampling. This statistical method accounts for animals that observers failed to detect and for differences in visibility across habitats. It produces an estimate of the population, rather than simply a tally of sightings. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest-running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said study co-author Dr. Nancy Bunbury. “By modeling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.” The animals were most concentrated in Aldabra’s grasslands, known as “tortoise turf.” The next highest densities occurred on open exposed surfaces and in open mixed scrub. Dense scrub, mangroves, and Pemphis vegetation made tortoises harder to detect. Correcting for those differences helps researchers distinguish places with fewer animals from places where animals are simply harder to spot. Together, the findings describe a population that has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable. They also establish a more dependable starting point for measuring future changes, something direct comparisons with older estimates cannot provide. Despite their recovery, Aldabra’s tortoises face growing environmental pressures. Droughts are projected to become longer and more frequent, reducing food and shade, while rising seas threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitats. Feral goats, which devastated Aldabra’s vegetation, were eradicated in 2012. But feral cats and black rats remain and prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The researchers say planned efforts to eliminate these mammals could allow more young tortoises to survive, support further population growth, and help the species withstand climate pressures. “These results are great news for the tortoises and a testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr. Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter in Cornwall who helped develop the statistical framework used to analyze the monitoring data. “But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline, not an endpoint. Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species.” Reference: “Inferring the Abundance of an Island Megaherbivore From Semi-Structured Distance Sampling” by Lara B. Hillyard, Nancy Bunbury, Christopher N. Kaiser-Bunbury, Dave Hodgson, Luke A’Bear, Cheryl L. Sanchez, Christopher W. Jones, April Burt, Frauke Fleischer-Dogley and Dave W. Hudson, 4 September 2026, Ecology and Evolution . DOI: 10.1002/ece3.74282 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .
ranking_reason: The study provides the first rigorous estimate of the Aldabra giant tortoise population, which has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable.

analysis.reason: The study provides the first rigorous estimate of the Aldabra giant tortoise population, which has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable.

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
content: Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday. In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker . "We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said. The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April. They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said. Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time. In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.
ranking_reason: The article reports a significant development in the field of AI, as a major financial institution like Bank of America acknowledges the need to patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced AI models, and the corresponding investment in human resources and financial resources.

analysis.reason: The article reports a significant development in the field of AI, as a major financial institution like Bank of America acknowledges the need to patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced AI models, and the corresponding investment in human resources and financial resources.

title: Huge data centre and solar farm plans revealed
content:
Plans have been drawn up for a huge new data centre and one of the UK's largest solar farms near King's Lynn in Norfolk.
Developers behind the Longmarsh Green Energy project said the data centre would require up to 1 gigawatt (GW) of power at any given time, while the solar farm the firm wants to build would generate up to 1.3GW.
Evolution Power Limited (EPL) said it was seeking to construct two sites covering around 4,695 acres (1,900 hectares) and the proposals could attract £25bn of investment.
A spokesperson said the project was "critical for future UK economic growth" and it had begun a consultation on the plans.
While details released about the project have been limited, the solar farm could generate more power than any other currently planned for the UK.
Developers behind the controversial High Grove scheme - one of the largest proposals which is also planned for rural Norfolk – say it would generate up to 720 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough for 363,000 homes.
That is just over half what the newly proposed site is said to be capable of producing.
The solar farm would also include battery storage.
Meanwhile the accompanying data centre would require up to 1GW of electricity at any one time.
EPL said one site for the project would be south of the A47 near the village of Tilney St Lawrence, with the other close to the villages of Fincham and Barton Bendish.
Along with drawing on solar energy, they would be connected to the existing electricity substation at Walpole, with the company aiming to have them operational by 2031.
It said the work would create thousands of construction jobs, while there would be more than 500 "direct operational roles" on site.
It added that it would use a "closed loop cooling system" – where liquid is recirculated – rather than taking water from the mains.
Such centres, which are used to store, process and transmit information, are frequently being opposed by local communities across the country, often due to environmental concerns.
But the government has deemed them critical to "nearly all economic activity and public services".
EPL said it expected to formally submit its planning application next April.
Because of its scale, it will be deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP), which means final say will rest with the government rather than the local council.
Other major schemes, such as High Grove, have also been classed as NSIPs.
Referring to that and projects including a large wind farm also planned for the area, North West Norfolk Conservative MP James Wild said the new plan "could represent further large scale industrialisation of the landscape".
Alistair Beales, the independent leader of King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council, said the authority would "do our job locally and reflect residents' concerns".
ranking_reason: The project could attract £25bn of investment and create thousands of construction jobs, making it a significant economic development.

analysis.reason: The project could attract £25bn of investment and create thousands of construction jobs, making it a significant economic development.
